title: Stress Signals
description: Physical actions the body takes to self-soothe when experiencing psychological discomfort.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: When the brain feels acute stress, it subconsciously directs the hands to stimulate nerve endings (usually near the face or neck) to naturally lower the heart rate. These are known as pacifying behaviors or self-soothing signals.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: Rubbing the back of the neck vigorously.
Tugging at a shirt collar or tie.
Stroking the face, rubbing the eyes, or touching the forehead.
Compressive lip biting (pulling the lips completely inward).
Wringing the hands or rapid foot tapping.

sections.title: What It May Indicate
content: High cognitive load (thinking incredibly hard or struggling to form an answer).
Psychological discomfort or generalized anxiety.
Nervousness strictly about being caught or exposed.
General environmental stress (feeling physically unsafe).

sections.title: What It Does NOT Mean
content: A stress signal does NOT equal guilt. An innocent person accused of a terrible crime will display massive stress signals.
A nose itch is NOT always a lie. Sometimes a nose is literally just itchy.
Fidgeting does NOT prove someone is hiding something; it is often just a release of excess baseline energy.

sections.title: Real Life Examples
content: Negotiation: A buyer starts aggressively rubbing the back of their neck when you firmly refuse to lower the price.
Workplace: An employee suddenly starts repeatedly clearing their throat before carefully answering a hard question about a missed deadline.
Police Interview: A suspect begins frantically dusting off completely invisible lint from their pants when a specific piece of evidence is verbally mentioned.

sections.title: Cluster Analysis
content: Rubbing neck + avoiding eye contact + sudden posture shift = High psychological discomfort.
Lip biting + rapid blinking + bouncing leg = Nervous anticipation.
Touching the face during a specific statement + changing vocal pitch = Potential indicator of deception related to that statement.

sections.title: Common Situations
content: High-stakes interrogations.
Public speaking.
Difficult emotional conversations.
Taking a high-pressure test or evaluation.

sections.title: Observation Mistakes
sections.content: Mistake: Assuming that because someone looks nervous, they must be lying. Reality: This is the 'Othello Error'. Truth-tellers often look nervous simply because they are afraid they won't be believed.

sections.title: Practical Observation Tips
content: Look strictly for the stimulus. What exact question or specific event caused the person to suddenly start stroking their face?
Identify their specific 'go-to' pacifier. Everyone has a favorite (some rub their neck, some play with a ring, some stroke their hair).
Watch exactly how long it takes them to generally calm down entirely after the stress signal.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: A massive, sudden explosion of pacifying behaviors (wringing hands, sweating, heavy breathing) in direct response to a seemingly innocent question.
Severe lip compression (lips sucked completely inward, disappearing) heavily indicating they are holding back something highly significant.
Ventilating (pulling at the shirt collar to let air out) strictly when a specific person is brought up.

sections.title: Reality Check
sections.content: The baseline matters most here. Some people are naturally anxious and fidget constantly. A stress signal only counts if it clearly departs from how someone behaves when comfortable.
